blocks.title: Secrets, Keys and Proof
blocks.subtitle: How mathematics protects messages and proves who sent them

blocks.text:
Every time a padlock appears in a browser, mathematics is doing something remarkable: two computers that have never met agree on a secret while the whole internet listens, and nobody else can learn it.

Cryptography provides secrecy, and also integrity and authenticity: proof that a message is unchanged and that it came from who it claims.

blocks.heading: Two families of cipher
blocks.text: A **symmetric** cipher uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt. It is fast, but the two sides must already share the key. A **public-key** system gives each party a pair of keys: a public one that anyone may know and a private one kept secret. Real protocols use public-key methods to agree a key, then a symmetric cipher for the data.

steps.text: **Exchange.** The two sides use a key-exchange method to derive a shared secret that an eavesdropper cannot compute.
**Encrypt.** A symmetric cipher such as AES scrambles the message with that secret key.
**Authenticate.** A message authentication code or digital signature is attached so tampering can be detected.
**Verify and decrypt.** The receiver checks the tag or signature, then decrypts with the shared key.

points.title: Key
points.text: The secret value that controls the transformation. Security rests on the key, not on hiding the algorithm.

points.title: Cipher
points.text: A public, well-studied algorithm such as AES or ChaCha20.

points.title: Ciphertext
points.text: The scrambled output, safe to send over an open channel.

points.title: Decryption
points.text: Applying the cipher with the right key to recover the plaintext.

blocks.heading: Hard problems as locks
blocks.text: Public-key cryptography depends on mathematical tasks that are easy one way and impractical to reverse, such as multiplying large primes versus factoring the result. A large quantum computer could solve some of these efficiently. **Post-quantum** algorithms based on different problems have therefore been standardised, and systems are beginning to migrate to them.

items.title: Symmetric encryption
items.text: One shared key for both directions; fast and used for bulk data.

items.title: Public-key cryptography
items.text: A public key to encrypt or verify, a private key to decrypt or sign.

items.title: Hash function
items.text: Maps any input to a fixed-length fingerprint that is impractical to reverse or collide.

items.title: Digital signature
items.text: Proof, made with a private key, that a message came from its owner unchanged.

items.title: Key exchange
items.text: A method for two parties to agree a secret over a public channel.

items.title: Certificate
items.text: A signed statement binding a public key to an identity.

blocks.heading: Where systems actually fail
blocks.text: Modern algorithms are rarely broken directly. Failures come from poor key management, weak random numbers, outdated protocol versions, implementation bugs and side channels such as timing. The practical rules are simple: use well-reviewed libraries, never invent your own cipher, protect and rotate keys, and plan the move to post-quantum algorithms.

items.title: Secure web
items.text: TLS protects browsing, banking and email in transit.

items.title: Payments
items.text: Cards and digital wallets authenticate transactions.

items.title: Digital identity
items.text: Signatures on documents, software and passports.

blocks.question: In public-key cryptography, which key must stay secret?
blocks.explanation: The public key can be shared freely. Only the private key can decrypt or sign.

blocks.question: What property makes a hash function useful for checking integrity?
options: It can be reversed with a key
Any change to the input changes the output unpredictably
blocks.explanation: A matching hash is strong evidence that the data are unchanged.

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**Plaintext / ciphertext**: a message before and after encryption. **Nonce**: a number used once. **MAC**: message authentication code. **TLS**: the protocol securing most internet connections. **Kerckhoffs's principle**: security should rest on the key alone.
